facts: At Stanford's Bing Nursery School in the late 1960s and early 1970s, Mischel's team led preschool children into a small room, called the Surprise Room in the book, and offered them a choice: one treat now, or a larger reward if they waited for the researcher to return.
The treats included marshmallows, cookies, little pretzels and mints. The researcher watched through a one-way window, and the child could ring a bell to end the wait.

Some children rang quickly. Others turned their backs to the treat, covered their eyes, sang quietly to themselves, played with their toes or whispered the rule to themselves; one sang about her home in Redwood City.
Children who imagined the treat was only a picture waited almost 18 minutes.
Mischel reports that those who waited longer at age 4 or 5 had higher SAT scores and were rated better socially and cognitively as adolescents.
Editorial caveat: later, larger studies found a smaller link between waiting and later outcomes once family background was taken into account.
Children who succeeded in waiting also pushed the bell away, repeated the two-treat rule aloud, or fell asleep; covering the treat made waiting easier (Times Higher Education review of the book).
A life-sized photo of the treat roughly doubled average waiting time, and telling children to frame the real treat as a picture produced the same gain; telling them the picture was real reversed it.

Mischel separates hot qualities of a treat (it tastes good, which triggers eating) from cool ones (white, soft), which help waiting. When he quit smoking he pictured a cancer patient receiving radiation whenever he craved a cigarette.

Mischel followed the children up years later: those who waited longer had more self-control and better social and cognitive functioning in adolescence (secondary: profiles say his daughters, who attended the school, started him asking how classmates fared).
scene_details: a line sung under the breath
tension: The children who waited did not stare harder at the treat; they looked away.
opening_idea: Open on the child with hands over eyes.

lessons.idea: Self-control works better as a way of managing what you look at than as straining against a pull, so change what is in front of you.
lessons.anchor: the children covering their eyes and singing

reflect_final: Which tempting thing could you put out of sight or change in your next hour at work or home, rather than resisting it?

use_cases.situation: You keep checking your phone in meetings.
use_cases.move: Put it in your bag before the meeting starts.

use_cases.situation: Your child is waiting for a treat.
use_cases.move: Suggest a song or a game to fill the wait.

use_cases.situation: You are avoiding a snack at your desk.
use_cases.move: Imagine the snack as something else, as the clouds in the study, or move it out of sight.

pocket_idea: The children who waited sang and covered their eyes: look away from the pull.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The children who waited longest were not staring at the marshmallow.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: At Stanford's Bing Nursery School, Walter Mischel offered children a marshmallow now or two later. Some waited by covering their eyes, singing, or even trying to sleep. When children were told to think of a marshmallow as a cloud, they waited longer. Mischel concluded waiting is about where attention goes.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What do you do to not look at a temptation?
